metadata.description: A collection of EAT-discovered, verified GPU kernels across hardware

readme.text:
EAT Kernels

Verified GPU kernels discovered by evolving agent teams

Fast, verified GPU kernels for LLM inference, packaged so engines can call them directly. Each kernel was discovered and optimized by agent teams evolved by [EAT](https://github.com/caoshiyi/EAT), and ships with: - its reference implementation and the benchmark it was measured with; - the recorded baseline numbers and the hardware it was tuned on; - known limitations, and a link to the full evolution traces. ## KDA (Kimi Delta Attention), head dim 128, varlen batches | directory | hardware | interface | ops | vs best prior kernel | |---|---|---|---|---| | [`kda/mi350x`](kda/mi350x) | AMD MI350X (gfx950) | **serving**: vLLM's ROCm Kimi-K3 calling convention (paged state pool, prefix-cache checkpoints, HIP graphs) | prefill + fused decode / speculative verify | prefill 3.04× vs vLLM ROCm; decode 1.69× vs the faster of AITER / vLLM HIP | | [`kda/b200`](kda/b200) | NVIDIA B200 (sm_100a) | **serving**: paged state pool, prefix-cache checkpoints, one CUDA graph across batch layouts; plain calls too | prefill | 2.57× vs FlashKDA (serving set, bf16 checkpoints; 2.40× fp32), 3.39× (Int21, H=64/96) | | [`kda/mi350x_plain`](kda/mi350x_plain) | AMD MI350X (gfx950) | plain calls (fla `chunk_kda` convention, contiguous state) | prefill | 3.01× vs vLLM ROCm, 7.3× vs fla Triton (H=12) | | [`kda/b200_plain`](kda/b200_plain) | NVIDIA B200 (sm_100a) | plain calls (benchmark track) | forward | 3.44× vs FlashKDA (Int21, H=64/96) | For an inference engine, use the **serving** kernel of your hardware. The `_plain` kernels are the earlier or benchmark-track versions on simpler interfaces, kept with their own results. Layout: `/[_]/`. Each directory holds the sources, a Python entry point, `reference.py`, a benchmark, tests and a `README.md` (API, results, limitations, provenance). License: Apache-2.0 (see NOTICE for third-party code).

metadata.description: EAT: Evolving Agent Teams (NeurIPS'26). A supervisor agent evolves teams of coding agents for long-running optimization tasks.

commit.message: README: M4 Pro GGUF numbers with victim pin + host tier lock

readme.text:
Evolving Agent Teams

Agents that diagnose why they stall and restructure their own team

One supervisor agent. No hand-written solution. It designs a team of coding agents, watches it work, diagnoses why it stalls, and rebuilds the team, for as long as the budget lasts.

## Get started In Claude Code, install EAT once: ``` /plugin install eat --marketplace caoshiyi/EAT ``` Then, in the repository you want to improve, just ask: > *Use EAT to make `bench.py` faster on GPUs 0 and 1. Budget $200.* > > *Run the EAT Gym task `amd_kda_mi350x` on GPUs 0-3 with a $300 budget.* Claude checks the machine, writes the task's eval and rules with you, records the starting score and launches the run; later ask it how the run is going, or to pause, stop or resume it. **Nothing installed?** Tell Claude Code *"Use EAT (github.com/caoshiyi/EAT) to ..."* and it fetches the skill itself. ## The supervisor invents the team that breaks the plateau The supervisor never touches the solution. When the score stalls, it reads the team's transcripts, names what is holding it back, and **creates the role that attacks it**. Over the 73 iterations of the MI350X run it used 42 distinct roles, from a single `solo_optimizer` to an `energy_auditor` and a `lander`:

**The B200 run passed the best published kernel in four iterations**, each one a team rebuilt around the supervisor's diagnosis of the last:

The same pattern appears late in long runs. In the MI350X run, iterations 57 and 58 shipped nothing; the supervisor found that the team had been timing its ideas in a different regime from the eval, and wrote a new role for iteration 59: > **ENERGY AUDITOR.** *"The pattern runs on a power transient: device time is 1.08–1.29× the gapped time ... The team > has therefore been pricing levers in a regime the score does not use. Your job is to fix the measurement and re-open > what it may have mis-judged."* That iteration set a new best (2.90×), and the run went on to 3.03×. Every team config, prompt and transcript is in the [traces](https://huggingface.co/datasets/eva98/eat-evolution-traces). ## Demos ### A robot policy written by agents The starting policy is the Pi_05 VLA. The EAT team replaced it with Python code that calls the frozen Pi_05 and, at runtime, Claude, and raised RoboDojo's leaderboard score from 11.4 to **62.1 on held-out seeds, above every entry on the leaderboard (55.3, Oct 26, 2026)**. Same scene, left: Pi_05; right: the team's code policy ([eat-robodojo-policy](https://github.com/caoshiyi/eat-robodojo-policy)).

make_kong (Mahjong): task score 16.7 → 97.2. Full video

arrange_largest_number: task score 2.5 → 88.3 classify_objects_by_language: task score 3.3 → 80.0
### Qwen3.8-Flash-Next served from a 48 GB Mac The model does not fit in the Mac's memory, so its experts stream from the SSD. An EAT team wrote the offload engine, starting from a naive port. - **Apple M5 Pro, 48 GB, GGUF UD-IQ4_XS**, against Strata on the same file at the same memory (peak 37.0 vs 37.2 GiB, both with MTP speculation, 262K context), **while keeping the KV cache in bf16 where Strata quantizes it to int8**: prefill **~3.3× faster** at every prompt length from 4K to 250K tokens (e.g. **910 vs 274 tokens/s** at 250K), decode **1.22× faster** after a short prompt (**43.7 vs 35.4 tokens/s**) and **1.21×** on AIME-25 requests; after a 250K-token prompt, decode is close (32.8 vs 30.1 tokens/s). - **Apple M4 Pro, 48 GB, MLX 4-bit** (the paper's task), against the naive engine: batch-1 decode **30.3 vs 13.4 tokens/s**, and recorded coding-agent sessions **3.32× faster**.

The same model driving Claude Code locally on the M5 Pro: each engine serves Claude Code v2.1.296, which adds CSV import and export to a small invoice library and writes the tests. Both pass their tests; over two runs each, EAT's engine takes **233 s** on average and Strata **386 s** (**1.66×**).

First run of each engine (3 min 29 s vs 5 min 49 s), each recorded alone and replayed side by side at 20× speed; the clock shows recorded time. Video

On the M4 Pro (GGUF, with the expert victim cache pinned and the host tier locked in memory, peak 44 GiB), the same engine decodes at 34.7 tokens/s after a short prompt and 30.2 tokens/s after a 250K-token prompt, and prefills at 350–375 tokens/s from 4K to 250K tokens. ## What is released - **Kernels**, packaged for inference engines (vLLM-style serving interface with paged state and prefix-cache checkpoints; MI350X 3.04× prefill and 1.69× decode, B200 2.57× on 26 serving workloads): [eat-kernels](https://github.com/caoshiyi/eat-kernels). - **The RoboDojo policy**, with its eval fleet setup: [eat-robodojo-policy](https://github.com/caoshiyi/eat-robodojo-policy). - **Every supervisor and agent transcript**, team config, note and per-iteration kernel or policy: [eva98/eat-evolution-traces](https://huggingface.co/datasets/eva98/eat-evolution-traces). - **The tasks**, at the state each run started from: [EAT Gym](https://huggingface.co/datasets/eva98/eat-gym). The Mac serving engine is not released yet: it is built on FreeToken-metal, which is not public; its code will follow once FreeToken-metal is open-sourced. ## How it works EAT is a harness in which a **supervisor** agent repeatedly designs, launches and revises a **team** of coding agents (Claude Code) that optimize a GPU kernel (or another program, such as a robot policy) against a fixed eval. The supervisor never writes the solution; its only output each iteration is a team configuration (roles, prompts, phases, ownership of files and GPUs). The team does the work, the harness runs the official eval, and the supervisor reflects on the result and evolves the team. A file system kept across all teams (learnings, evolution history, artifacts) grounds each redesign in what earlier teams found.

``` while budget remains: supervisor: REFLECT on the previous team's output -> EVOLVE roles / prompts / workflow -> emit TEAM_CONFIG harness: launch the team's agents phase by phase -> run the official eval -> record cost and score ``` ## Clean-room runs To show that a result was not copied from code released after a cutoff, run the whole loop inside the [bubblewrap](https://github.com/containers/bubblewrap) sandbox, from the task repository: ```bash EAT_CLEAN=/path/to/sandbox-state EAT_ALLOWED_RO="/refs/cutlass /refs/flashinfer-2026-08-13" EAT_GPUS="0 1" \ CLAUDE_EXTRA_DISALLOWED=WebSearch,WebFetch $EAT_HOME/cleanroom/sandbox.sh \ bash $EAT_HOME/agent_team/launch_stateless.sh --persistent 50 3 300 ``` Only the task repository, EAT, and the `EAT_ALLOWED_RO` sources are visible, and the network reaches only the Anthropic API (through `allowlist_proxy.py`, which logs every request). Afterwards, `cleanroom/audit_clean_traces.py` scans every tool call in the run's transcripts for web use, network commands and forbidden sources, and `cleanroom/audit_code_overlap.py` finds code lines that appear only in the forbidden sources. ## For coding agents If a user asks you to use EAT and the `eat` skill is not installed: clone this repository (for example to `~/.claude/skills/eat`) and follow [`SKILL.md`](SKILL.md), with `EAT_HOME` set to the clone. ## Citation ```bibtex @inproceedings{cao2026eat, title = {Evolving Agent Teams}, author = {Cao, Shiyi and Mao, Ziming and Li, Dacheng and Gonzalez, Joseph E. and Stoica, Ion}, booktitle = {Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)}, year = {2026}, url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36848} } ``` ## License Apache-2.0. Tasks installed from the EAT Gym bring their own NOTICE for the third-party code they contain.

metadata.description: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (552B MoE + 196B Engram) on 2x RTX 3090 + 128 GB RAM. Rust + CUDA, T16 quantization. 40+ tok/s measured with expert deferral + FP8 projections.

commit.message:
quant/README: link the published calib4 set (lxe/dsx-calibration)

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

readme.text:
dsx

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (552 B + 196 B Engram) on your old gaming PC
two RTX 3090s and 128 GB of RAM · 40+ tokens/s decode · 1,000+ tokens/s prefill measured · full routing, no expert pruning · OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible API · chat in the browser, pictures, thinking levels

dsx runs **[DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017)** locally on two RTX 3090s and 128 GB of RAM. It is a Rust and CUDA inference engine with a T16 quantized model, a browser chat UI, image input, and OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs for coding agents. The [current model](https://huggingface.co/lxe/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-dsx-t16) is a single 252 GB GGUF with the experts, Engram memory and tokenizer included. The download also supplies the expert ranking and a separate vision tower. [T16](docs/t16-format.md) uses a trellis format designed for both desktop CPU and GPU execution. ## Quick start The reference machine has two 24 GB RTX 3090s, an i7-12700K, 128 GB of RAM and an NVMe drive with about 255 GB free. You need Rust, CUDA 13 and an x86 CPU with AVX2; AVX-VNNI or AVX-512 VNNI is preferred. Download the model and build the NVIDIA runner: ```bash hf download lxe/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-dsx-t16 --local-dir dsx-t16 CUDA_ARCHS=86 cargo build --release -p dsx --features cuda ``` Use `CUDA_ARCHS=89` for an RTX 4090 or `120` for an RTX 5090. **`CUDA_ARCHS=70` runs on Tesla V100 (Volta) — see [Tesla V100](#tesla-v100-sm70).** ### Tesla V100 (SM70) `CUDA_ARCHS=70` (with CUDA 12.9) builds for Volta: every SM80-only kernel has an SM70 twin, and SM80+ binaries are unchanged. Measured on 2x V100-PCIE-32GB with 108 GB of RAM: 21-23 tokens/s decode and 467 tokens/s prefill on a 123K-token prompt. Details and checks: [bench/results/2026-11-01-volta](bench/results/2026-11-01-volta/README.md). ```bash CUDA_ARCHS=70 cargo build --release -p dsx --features cuda DSX_GPUS=0,1 ./target/release/dsx-server --model dsx-t16/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-dsx-t16.gguf \ --rank dsx-t16/expert-rank.json --main-gb=-2.0 --arena-gb 85 --ctx 131072 ``` Start the server: ```bash ./target/release/dsx-server \ --model dsx-t16/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-dsx-t16.gguf \ --rank dsx-t16/expert-rank.json \ --ctx 131072 \ --arena-gb 110 \ --defer-rank 3 \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8090 ``` Open **http://localhost:8090/** for the chat UI. The server loads `vision.safetensors` beside the model for image input. Use `--no-vision` for text only. `--defer-rank 3` lets lower-ranked CPU experts finish one layer late to reduce GPU waiting. It changes the model’s computation; omit the flag to disable that approximation. See [server configuration](docs/server.md) for all options and [expert placement](docs/placement.md) for other memory and GPU configurations. Or build and run the same server in Docker (NVIDIA Container Toolkit required). The default image carries sm_86, sm_89 and sm_120 kernels; `--build-arg CUDA_ARCHS=86` narrows the fatbin to one GPU: ```bash docker build -t dsx . docker run --gpus all --ipc=host --ulimit memlock=-1:-1 \ -v "$PWD/dsx-t16:/models:ro" -p 8090:8090 dsx \ --model /models/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-dsx-t16.gguf \ --rank /models/expert-rank.json --ctx 131072 --arena-gb 110 \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8090 ``` `--target amd` builds the MI325X runner instead. ## Coding agents and API Point an OpenAI-compatible client at `http://localhost:8090/v1`, or an Anthropic-compatible client at `http://localhost:8090`. The model ID is `deepseek-v4.1-flash`. For [Pi](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono), follow the [provider setup](docs/agents.md), then run: ```bash pi --provider dsx --model deepseek-v4.1-flash:off ``` Thinking is on at high effort by default. Requests can turn it off or choose another effort. For example: ```bash curl http://localhost:8090/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{ "model": "deepseek-v4.1-flash", "stream": true, "reasoning_effort": "none", "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Write a Python function that merges sorted iterators."} ] }' ``` The default sampling is temperature 1 and top-p 1. [Thinking controls](docs/server.md#thinking) cover both APIs. Use `--api-key` to require authentication. ## Performance On the reference two-3090 machine, a T16 free-generation run measured **41.0 tokens/s** with `--defer-rank 3` and optional FP8 Engram projections (`DSX_ENGRAM_FP8=1`). FP8 projections are off by default. This was a 120-token run after 300 tokens; throughput depends on context length, expert routing and cache warm-up. The October 25 prefill checkpoint measured **1,008 tokens/s** on an 8,000-token prompt with an 8K chunk, 256K context allocation and the same T16 weights. The [prefill profile and receipts](bench/results/2026-10-25-prefill/README.md) cover the opt-in kernels, buffer reuse, warm-up and expert placement. This is a separate measurement from the 41 tokens/s generation result above; smaller prompt updates have different throughput. The [measurement record](docs/current-state.md) gives build identities, quality measurements and open checks. ## How it works The model selects six of its 384 experts in each layer. dsx keeps frequently used experts on the GPUs and computes the remaining selected experts on the CPU from RAM. The CPU and GPUs work in parallel, and the main GPU combines their results. An adaptive cache follows the experts used by the current conversation. At startup, dsx measures each GPU’s memory and host-link speed to assign its role. During prefill, experts stream from RAM over the available fast links. Follow-up requests reuse the cached conversation prefix so only new text needs prefill. [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) describes the execution and memory layout. ## Documentation | Guide | Contents | |---|---| | [Server configuration](docs/server.md) | Model files, authentication, sampling, thinking and runtime flags | | [Coding agents](docs/agents.md) | Pi provider configuration | | [Expert placement](docs/placement.md) | GPU, RAM and disk placement; tuning for your machine | | [T16 format](docs/t16-format.md) | Quantization and CPU/GPU decoding | | [Overlays](docs/overlays.md) | Small GGUFs that replace a few tensors at load, such as the uncensored overlay | | [NVIDIA runner](nvidia/README.md) | CLI tools, build details and debugging | | [AMD runner](amd/README.md) | The separate MI325X implementation and model | | [Measurements](docs/current-state.md) | Current runtime status, quality evidence and benchmark history | | [Findings](FINDINGS.md) | Detailed experiments and optimization results | MIT license. See [credits](CREDITS.md) for upstream projects, model sources and attribution.

BF16 GEMV at1182 is warp-per-row vector loads with FP32 dot; no comparable Muse performance evidence. Optional expert deferral explicitly changes computation. No compatible demonstrated improvement.

readme.text:
volta

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (552 B + 196 B Engram) on one used 8x V100 server
2,400-3,000 tokens/s across hundreds of sessions · DSpark speculative decoding · OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible API · thinking levels, streaming, prefix reuse

An 8x V100 machine (the DGX-1 NVLink layout, 256 GB of HBM) is old and cheap, and no serving engine runs **[DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017)** (DeepSeek, MIT license) on it: Volta has no FP8, FP4 or bf16 math, and the official checkpoint is larger than its memory. Together the eight cards still read 6.9 TB/s. volta is an engine in Rust and CUDA, written for this one model on this one class of machine, that turns that bandwidth into throughput for many sessions at once. - **Fast:** 2,400 tokens/s across 256 sessions and 3,070 across 512; 24 tokens/s per session with 64 at once. A single session decodes 53 tokens/s, and 76 with `--head-parallel` (~230 on code with the draft). - **Close to the original:** the same next token as the FP8 model 84% of the time on the Lucebox eval (KL 0.127). - **Faster with the draft model:** the checkpoint's DSpark draft runs on the GPUs. With 64 sessions writing code, each gets 27 tokens/s instead of 20, and sampled outputs keep the model's own distribution (speculative sampling). - **Plugs into your tools:** the OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible API of [dsx](https://github.com/lxe/dsx), with streaming, tools, thinking levels and the chat in the browser. - **Long context:** 128K tokens per session for 16 sessions at once (256K with one per GPU). The compressed KV cache is stored as FP4, ~0.9 KB per token. - **Picks up where you left off:** a finished session's KV cache stays on the GPU, so an agent that resends the whole conversation only pays for the new text. ## The model https://huggingface.co/lxe/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-Volta The Hugging Face repository contains one complete `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-Volta.gguf` model file, about 442 GB. It includes the unchanged base tensors, Engram tables, draft and vision weights, tokenizer and model configuration, together with the 220 GB of quantized main routed experts. No separate base directory or tokenizer file is required. The experts use cb3 (15,172 experts, 3.25 bits per weight) and cb2 (188 cold experts, 2.25 bits), chosen by how often the router picks them. The [GGUF format](docs/portable-quant.md) stores row-major expert codes and scale bytes. The engine reconstructs its kernel layout at load while preserving the quantized values and original eight-way source slices. The file uses custom Volta encoding metadata and requires this engine. It is not a llama.cpp quant type. Previously downloaded native expert packs and base directories remain supported. The complete GGUF also has [GPU validation and four-agent measurements from October 24, 2026](docs/benchmarks/2026-10-24-v100/README.md), including actual Pi tool use, live tmux shapes, 128K/256K retrieval checks and controlled sampler comparisons. The data-parallel 128K profile measured 165.2–169.3 aggregate whole-request tokens/s for four cold 4K-input/1,024-output requests. It remains the measured throughput choice for four short-task agents. For head-parallel serving, `VOLTA_HP_GPU_SAMPLE=1` opts into collecting the eight vocabulary slices on GPU0 and using the existing GPU sampler. Four-client, 256K-capacity A/B/B/A tests measured 51.8–53.9% higher fixed-workload throughput and 47.8–47.9% higher mixed prefill/decode throughput than CPU HP sampling. The [HP receipts](docs/benchmarks/2026-10-24-v100/hp-gpu-sampling/) retain the real-row audit, quality checks, fallbacks and different CPU/GPU sampling trajectories. Default HP sampling is unchanged. The quality and performance results below were measured with the original native pack, before the GGUF repack. Against the FP8 model on the [Lucebox](https://huggingface.co/Lucebox/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-ROCMFP-GGUF) eval (8 x 1,024 tokens), it picks the same next token 84.1% of the time, with KL 0.127 and perplexity 8.88. ## How fast is it? All on one 8x V100-SXM2-32GB machine. Engine benchmark (`volta bench`, real text, one token per session per step): | Sessions | Step | Total | |---|---|---| | 64 | 41.7 ms | 1,536 tok/s | | 128 | 69 ms | 1,850 tok/s | | 256 | 105 ms | 2,440 tok/s | | 512 | 167 ms | 3,070 tok/s | With the DSpark draft (`volta spec --adaptive`, greedy, 64 sessions): 28.4 tok/s per session on code and 18.2 on prose. With 8 sessions on code: 81 tok/s each. One session (`volta spec`, greedy, steady-state step): | Mode | Step | Per session | With the draft, on code | |---|---|---|---| | default (attention on the session's GPU) | 17.8 ms | 56 tok/s | 200 tok/s | | `--head-parallel` (every GPU, 8 heads each) | 10.7 ms | 94 tok/s | 277 tok/s | With `--head-parallel`, 4 sessions with the draft on code get 114 tok/s each. Through the server (`volta-server`, sampling at temperature 1 with drafts, 300-token answers; up to 8 streams with `--slots 1 --ctx 131072`, 32 with `--slots 4 --ctx 32768`): | Concurrent streams | Per stream | Total | First token | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 93 tok/s | 84 tok/s | 0.33 s | | 8 | 72 tok/s | 343 tok/s | 0.5 s | | 32 | 39 tok/s | 967 tok/s | 1.0 s | Long prompts (`volta spec`, 8 sessions, one per GPU, code, with drafts): with 64K-token prompts, prefill runs at 2,490 tok/s in total and decoding at 71 tok/s per session; with 128K-token prompts, at 1,430 and 46. The compressed KV cache is stored as FP4, ~0.9 KB per token per session, so `--slots 2 --ctx 131072` gives 16 sessions of 128K. For comparison, llama.cpp (PR #30817, UD-IQ1_M) on the same machine decodes 26.7 tok/s for one stream and 72-97 tok/s in total at most. ## Quick start Download the complete model (~442 GB): ```bash hf download lxe/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-Volta --local-dir volta-weights ``` Build and start the server: ```bash NVCC=/usr/local/cuda-12.9/bin/nvcc CUDA_ARCHS=70 cargo build --release -p dsx --features cuda --bin volta-server ./target/release/volta-server \ --model volta-weights/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-Volta.gguf \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8090 ``` That serves 32 sessions of 8,192 tokens. For agents with long conversations, trade sessions for context: `--slots 2 --ctx 131072` serves 16 sessions of 128K, and `--slots 1 --ctx 262144` 8 sessions of 256K. For the fastest single sessions, add `--head-parallel`: every GPU runs every session with 8 of the 64 attention heads, so the machine holds `--slots` sessions in total instead of `--slots` per GPU, each at up to ~94 tok/s without the draft. Every GPU keeps a copy of each session's KV cache, so `--slots` and `--ctx` share memory as they do without the flag. Loading reconstructs the expert kernel layout and maps the 196 GB Engram tables into RAM. Full-model startup time for the GGUF path has not been measured. Open `http://localhost:8090/` for the web UI, or point any OpenAI client at `http://localhost:8090/v1` (Anthropic clients at `http://localhost:8090`): ```bash curl http://localhost:8090/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{ "model": "deepseek-v4.1-flash", "stream": true, "reasoning_effort": "none", "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Write a haiku about MoE routing."} ] }' ``` An admin dashboard runs on `http://localhost:8091/`: output and prompt throughput (live and over the last 5 minutes), sessions in use, speed per session, drafts kept, step time, and the active and recently finished requests. The same numbers are JSON at `/stats`. To use the official checkpoint instead of the complete GGUF, pass the checkpoint directory as `--model`: the engine packs the experts on the GPUs at load (~3 minutes) and caches them in `/dev/shm/vcache`. ### Agents For the [pi](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono) coding agent, add this to `~/.pi/agent/models.json`: ```json { "providers": { "volta": { "baseUrl": "http://localhost:8090/v1", "api": "openai-completions", "apiKey": "none", "authHeader": false, "compat": { "supportsDeveloperRole": false, "supportsReasoningEffort": true, "maxTokensField": "max_tokens" }, "models": [ { "id": "deepseek-v4.1-flash", "reasoning": true, "input": ["text"], "contextWindow": 131072, "maxTokens": 16384, "thinkingLevelMap": { "off": "none", "high": "high" } } ] } } } ``` ```bash pi --provider volta --model deepseek-v4.1-flash:off ``` `contextWindow` must match the server's `--ctx` (here `--slots 2 --ctx 131072 --max-tokens 16384`). pi compacts long conversations by itself (it summarizes older messages when the context is nearly full). To start compaction with room for a full answer and keep more recent history, add this to `~/.pi/agent/settings.json`: ```json { "compaction": { "enabled": true, "modelOverrides": { "volta/deepseek-v4.1-flash": { "reserveTokens": 20480, "keepRecentTokens": 32768 } } } } ``` The server's prefix cache reuses everything before the summary, so the first request after a compaction only reads the summary and the messages kept after it. With `--api-key`: drop `"authHeader": false`, set `"apiKey"` to the key and point `baseUrl` at the server's URL. ## Requirements | | | |---|---| | GPUs | 8x V100 32 GB with NVLink in the DGX-1 layout (SXM2 or SXM3) | | CUDA | 12.9 (the last toolkit that builds for sm_70) | | RAM | ~400 GB (the Engram tables, 196 GB, are read from RAM) | | Disk | ~442 GB for the Hugging Face build; use fast storage for the model file | Other machines need other kernels and collectives; [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) lists what each would take. ## Parameters `volta-server` needs `--model`; every other option has a default. **Model files** | | | |---|---| | `--model` | the complete Volta GGUF, or a checkpoint/base directory | | `VOLTA_PACK` | optional expert override for directory models: GGUF or native pack (original GPU topology required) | | `--tokenizer` | `tokenizer.json`; default: the model directory's | **Server** | | | |---|---| | `--host`, `--port` | listen address (default `127.0.0.1:8090`) | | `--api-key` | require this key (`Authorization: Bearer ` or `x-api-key`; env `DSX_API_KEY`) | | `--model-name` | model id reported by `/v1/models` (default `deepseek-v4.1-flash`) | | `--slots` | concurrent sessions per GPU (default 4); with `--head-parallel`, in total | | `--head-parallel` | every GPU runs every session with 8 of the 64 attention heads and a copy of its KV cache: the fastest single sessions, for fewer of them | | `--ctx` | context window per session, prompt + generated tokens (default 8192); slots and context share the GPUs' spare memory: 2 x 131072 fits | | `--max-tokens` | generation cap when a request sets none (default 4096) | | `--chunk` | prompt tokens per session per step while reading a prompt (default 32) | | `--admin-port` | the admin dashboard and `/stats` (default 8091, on `--host`; 0 = off). It has no API key: keep it on loopback or a private network | **Sampling defaults** (a request's own fields override them) | | | |---|---| | `--temperature`, `--top-p` | default 1.0 and 1.0, the model's recommended sampling | | `--hesitation-penalty` | logit penalty on hesitation tokens ("Wait", "But", ...) while reasoning; 0 = off (default) | **Draft** | | | |---|---| | `--spec-k` | most draft tokens verified per pass (default 5; 0 turns the draft off) | | `--theta` | a session verifies j drafts while p^j >= theta, p = its recent per-draft acceptance (default 0.35) | ## Thinking Thinking is on by default, at high effort. A request turns it off or sets the effort: | | OpenAI API (`/v1/chat/completions`) | Anthropic API (`/v1/messages`) | |---|---|---| | Thinking off | `"reasoning_effort": "none"` or `"thinking": {"type": "disabled"}` | `"thinking": {"type": "disabled"}` | | Effort | `"reasoning_effort"`: `low` (or `minimal`), `high` (or `medium`), `xhigh`, `max` | `"output_config": {"effort": ...}`: `low`, `high` (or `medium`), `xhigh`, `max` | ## How it works The model has 15,360 routed experts (384 in each of its 40 layers); each token uses 6 per layer, plus a shared expert, attention, and two Engram lookups. Every step runs all sessions' tokens together. - **Every expert split 8 ways:** each GPU holds 1/8 of every expert's weights (and of the shared expert), so every GPU does the same work in every layer, whichever experts the router picks. - **Formats made for the hardware:** each expert's MXFP4 weights become cb3 or cb2 codes. The kernel turns two weights into fp16 with one shared-memory lookup and feeds Volta's `mma.m8n8k4` tensor cores directly. The dense weights are 4-bit with an fp16 scale per 16. - **Attention per GPU, experts across all of them:** each GPU keeps its own sessions' KV cache and runs their attention and dense layers. Per layer, one NVLink all-gather sends every token's hidden state to every GPU, and one all-to-all brings the partial sums home. Both are single kernels that write into peer memory and signal with flags (~13-17 µs each). - **Head-parallel for few sessions:** with `--head-parallel` each GPU runs 8 of the 64 heads (one of the model's 8 output groups) of every session, so a token's dense attention weights are read once across the GPUs instead of whole on one. The attention output and the MoE partials are summed on every GPU in a fixed order, so all eight hold the same bits and route to the same experts; small exchanges use NCCL-style LL words (data and sequence number in one 8-byte store), 5-8 µs. - **Attention on the tensor cores:** one KV row serves all 64 query heads, so a token's attention is a matrix product, run with `mma.m8n8k4` in fp16. The indexer that picks each token's 512 compressed rows scores them on the tensor cores too. - **KV cache in FP4:** the model rounds its compressed KV rows and indexer keys to FP4, so they are stored packed, exactly: ~0.9 KB per token per session, 0.23 GB for a 256K-token context. - **One CUDA graph per step:** routing is built on the GPU, small kernels are merged, and independent work (the shared expert, the larger expert batches) runs on a second stream inside the graph. - **Several tokens per session per step:** prompts are read in chunks, and the draft's tokens are verified, in the same step as everyone else's decoding. - **DSpark on the GPUs:** the checkpoint's 3-layer draft runs through the same MoE path. Each session verifies as many drafts as its recent acceptance justifies; every GPU verifies the same number of tokens per step, so the step stays in a CUDA graph. [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) has the design, the measurements behind each choice, and the time per step by kernel. ## Command-line tools `volta` (`--bin volta`) runs the engine without the server: | | | |---|---| | `volta bench --model ... --sessions 8 --steps 32 --text tokens.i32` | throughput with `--sessions` per GPU; `--text` feeds real tokens (i32 LE) | | `volta eval --model ... --eval ` | the Lucebox eval; `--chunk k` feeds k tokens per sequence per step | | `volta spec --model ... --text tokens.i32 --k 5 --adaptive` | greedy decoding with the draft (`VOLTA_SPARK=`); `--total N` for N sessions in all | | `volta check`, `volta experts` | logits and expert kernels against the CPU reference | | Variable | Effect | |---|---| | `VOLTA_EXPERT_GB` | expert bytes per GPU when packing from the official checkpoint (default 25; the published pack is 27.5) | | `VOLTA_GRAPHS` | most step shapes kept as CUDA graphs (the server's default is 4) | | `VOLTA_TRACE_STEP` | wraps that step in a profiler range, for `nsys --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi` | | `VOLTA_PROF` | prints where each step's time went | | `VOLTA_OVERLAP=0`, `VOLTA_ATTN=tile5`, `VOLTA_SPARK_CB2=0` | one stream, CUDA-core attention, cb3 draft experts | | `VOLTA_KV=bf16` | store the compressed KV cache in bf16 instead of FP4 (3.5x larger) | ## Next - A 256K-context run with 8 head-parallel sessions and the most drafts per step. - Volta Scout's expert kernel (vlut2: gate/up 31 -> 19 us at one token in the lab, same bits) with the shared-expert slice moved beside the router (`VOLTA_SHARED_EARLY=1`), so the expert pass has the GPU to itself. - The routing chain folded into the router's last block (built in the lab, not yet measured). - The MoE exchange and the down projection, the remaining per-layer costs above their floors (DESIGN.md). - A router process in front of the server, so sampling settings change without a restart. ## Repo | Path | | |---|---| | [`engine/src/volta.rs`](engine/src/volta.rs), [`engine/src/volta/spark.rs`](engine/src/volta/spark.rs) | the engine: packing, placement, steps, attention, MoE, collectives, CUDA graphs; the draft | | [`engine/src/kernels/volta.cuh`](engine/src/kernels/volta.cuh) | the sm_70 kernels | | [`engine/src/server/volta.rs`](engine/src/server/volta.rs), [`engine/src/bin/volta_server.rs`](engine/src/bin/volta_server.rs) | the batching scheduler and the server | | [`engine/src/server/telemetry.rs`](engine/src/server/telemetry.rs), [`engine/src/server/dashboard.html`](engine/src/server/dashboard.html) | the admin dashboard's numbers and page | | [`core/`](core/), the rest of [`engine/`](engine/) | model loader, CPU reference, the HTTP server and web UI, from [dsx](https://github.com/lxe/dsx) | | [`plans/`](plans/) | the published pack's tier plan and placement, and the routing counts that choose tiers | | [`tests/`](tests/) | standalone kernel tests against reference kernels: expert formats (`vmoe_test`, `vlut_test`), dense and expert launch shapes (`dense_test`, `split_test`), attention (`attn_test`), indexer (`indexer_test`) | | [`bench/`](bench/) | hardware probes and the existing-engine benchmarks | ## Credits [DeepSeek](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai) for the model (MIT) · [dsx](https://github.com/lxe/dsx) for the model loader, CPU reference, server and web UI · [Lucebox](https://huggingface.co/Lucebox/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-ROCMFP-GGUF) for the eval set · the web UI is [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp)'s, by Georgi Gerganov and the ggml authors (MIT), vendored in [`core/webui`](core/webui) with its license. MIT license.

readme.text:
# pocket-engine

An inference server for Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.8 models, written from scratch in Rust and CUDA, with an OpenAI-compatible chat API. Runs on NVIDIA GPUs and on AMD's MI325X.

- **[Starts in 2 to 3 seconds.](docs/design.md#one-process-no-python)** A single Rust binary, no Python.
- **Fast first tokens.** 13.5 ms for a short prompt on an H100.
- **[Speculative decoding](docs/design.md#speculative-decoding)** with Qwen's built-in prediction layer. Same answers as without it, nearly twice as fast: 293 tokens/s for one 9B request on an H100.
- **[Drafting from the prompt.](docs/design.md#speculative-decoding)** Up to 4 times faster when answers quote or edit their input.
- **[Prefix caching for hybrid models.](docs/design.md#prefix-cache)** Each turn of a chat reuses the last one's work.
- **[GGUF support.](docs/design.md#quantized-weights)** Serve the quantized files you already have from llama.cpp, with no conversion, at 2,372 tokens/s for 9B on an RTX 5090.
- **[Load and serve adapters on a live server.](docs/design.md#lora-adapters)** Add or remove a fine-tune without a restart, while requests for the base model keep full speed.
- **bf16, FP8, FP4 and GGUF weights;** JSON output, log-probabilities and images.

Output tokens per second against vLLM 0.31.0 on the same GPU model. Each cell shows one request / 64 requests at once.

| GPU | Model | pocket-engine | vLLM |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| B200 | Qwen3.5-9B | **230** / **5,408** | 224 / 4,782 |
| B200 | Qwen3.8-27B | 86 / 1,766 | **87** / **1,803** |
| H100 | Qwen3.5-9B | **150** / **3,534** | 143 / 2,567 |
| H100 | Qwen3.8-27B | **50** / 1,069 | 45 / **1,092** |
| MI325X | Qwen3.5-9B | **225** / **4,103** | 207 / 3,273 |
| MI325X | Qwen3.8-27B | 74 / **1,269** | **76** / 1,166 |

All bf16. More GPUs and formats, first-token times, and the runs behind every number are in [benchmarks](docs/benchmarks.md).

## Quick start

Requires Rust 1.98 or newer and either an NVIDIA GPU with driver 580 or newer and the CUDA 13 toolkit, or an AMD MI325X with ROCm 7 (hipcc, HIP and hipBLAS).

```sh
git clone https://github.com/lxe/pocket-engine && cd pocket-engine
CUDA_COMPUTE_CAP=90a cargo build --release --features cuda   # 100a for B200, 120a for RTX 50-series
# cargo build --release --features rocm                       # AMD MI325X (gfx942), ROCm 7

hf download Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B --local-dir models/qwen3.5-2b
target/release/pocket-engine serve --model models/qwen3.5-2b --bind 0.0.0.0:8000
```

```sh
curl localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model": "qwen3.5-2b", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]}'
```

## Supported

- **Models:** Qwen3.5 0.8B, 2B, 4B and 9B, and Qwen3.8-27B, with images. Dense models only.
- **GPUs:** H100, H200, B200 and RTX 50-series; AMD MI325X (ROCm).
- **Weights:** bf16, FP8, FP4 (RTX 50-series) and GGUF.
- **Adapters:** PEFT and llama.cpp LoRA, over any of those weights.

## Documentation

- [Usage](docs/usage.md): API, sampling, server options, weight formats
- [Benchmarks](docs/benchmarks.md): every GPU, model and format, against vLLM
- [Design](docs/design.md): how it works, from scheduling to kernels
- [Accuracy](docs/accuracy.md): comparisons with Transformers
- [Testing](docs/testing.md): running the test suite

## License

MIT

No MoE or matched Muse performance result found.

readme.text:
# gpu-anatomy

Hands-on experiments touching every part of an NVIDIA GPU. One folder per hardware unit, one `.cu` file per experiment.

A companion **UI walkthrough** is available to follow these experiments in order with explanations: [link TBD].

## What's in here

Folders covered so far:

- `01-global-memory/`: coalesced vs strided vs random access, vectorized loads, sector utilization
- `02-shared-memory/`: bank conflicts (2-way, 32-way), padding, swizzling, shared atomics
- `03-registers/`: register count vs occupancy, spilling to local memory
- `04-warp-behavior/`: divergence, predication, branch uniformity
- `05-warp-shuffle/`: broadcast, reduce, prefix scan
- `09-tensor-cores/`: WMMA FP16 matmul
- `10-async-copy/`: `cp.async`, double-buffered pipelining
- `18-rt-cores/`: OptiX, BVH traversal, ray-triangle (renders a real image)

## Building

```bash
make
```

Builds every `.cu` into `bin/<folder>/<name>`. OptiX experiments
(`18-rt-cores/`) only build if `OPTIX_HOME` is set: see that folder's
README for setup.

Build a single experiment:
```bash
make bin/03-registers/forced_spill
```

## Running

```bash
./bin/03-registers/forced_spill
```

Most files have an ncu command in their bottom comment block to reproduce
the measurements.

## Dependencies

- CUDA toolkit (tested with 13.x)
- NVIDIA driver new enough for your GPU
- `nvidia-smi`, `ncu`, `cuobjdump` (ship with CUDA)
- For `18-rt-cores/` only: NVIDIA OptiX SDK
